units.text: MAPPING THE GALACTIC HALO. IV. FINDING DISTANT GIANTS RELIABLY WITH THE WASHINGTON SYSTEM
INTRODUCTION

Photometric searches over wide areas for rare, distant giants in the Galactic halo are now a reality, thanks to the advent of wide-Ðeld CCD systems. One particularly useful photometric system is the Washington system (Canterna 1976 ;Harris & Canterna 1979). Since Geisler (1984) added the DDO 51 Ðlter to allow discrimination between late-type dwarfs and giants and recalibrated its [Fe/H] indicator, this system has steadily gained in popularity. Its broadband Ðlters and strong abundance sensitivity for late-type giants (Geisler, Claria, & Minniti 1991 ;Paltoglou & Bell 1994) mean that it was well suited to studies of objects of known distance such as open and globular cluster giants. In these cases there is little need for luminosity discrimination.
However, when seeking rare objects such as halo giants, which are seen through a thick veil of foreground disk stars, ÈÈÈÈÈÈÈÈÈÈÈÈÈÈÈ 1 Cottrell Scholar of Research Corporation and NSF CAREER fellow.

luminosity discrimination is vital. The Mg b/MgH feature near 5170 is strong in late-type dwarfs and weak in giants. A The DDO51 Ðlter (with and *j \ 154 is j c \ 5130 A A ) centered on this feature. It works well for discriminating between late GÈK dwarfs of solar or near-solar metallicity and GÈK giants. The addition of this Ðlter has allowed the use of the Washington system in surveys for late G and K giants where foreground contamination by disk dwarfs is a problem. This is superior to other photometric methods of identifying giants, such as DDO or photometry Stro mgren (McClure & Forrester 1981 ;Bond 1980), because only one Ðlter has a narrow passband, and it is not necessary to observe in the ultraviolet. Surveys well suited to the Washington system include 1. Studies of giant stars in clusters at low latitude, where it is now possible to remove foreground dwarf nonmembers (e.g., Geisler, Claria, & Minniti 1997) ; 2. Surveys for rare Ðeld giants of the outer halo (Morrison et al. 2000, hereafter Paper I ;Majewski et al. 2000a, hereafter MOPK) ; 3. Surveys for extratidal giants from Galactic dwarf satellites (Majewski et al. 1999 ;Majewski et al. 2000b, herafter MOPKJG).

The last two types of survey make contributions to our understanding of the formation and subsequent evolution of the Galaxy. Distant halo Ðeld giants, such as the one recently discovered by our survey at 80 kpc (Olszewski et al. 2001) provide in situ probes of the outer halo and are also important probes of the Galactic potential (Zaritsky et al. 1989). But their identiÐcation as giants must be solid to make them useful ; the spatial distribution and kinematics of local halo dwarfs will contribute little to our understanding of the outer Galaxy. Indeed, misidentiÐcation will lead to serious errors.

We began work on this paper to understand our low success rate at identifying halo giants for V magnitudes fainter than 18. For brighter magnitudes our success rate, conÐrmed by spectroscopic follow-up, is better than 90%, but this falls precipitously to 24% for V magnitudes between 18 and 19  ; hereafter Paper II), despite comparably good mean photometric uncertainties for these fainter stars.

A detailed investigation into the limitations of the Washington luminosity classiÐcation may also cast light on some surprising claims from the surveys around dwarf satellites of the Milky Way. For example, MOPKJG have claimed detection of large numbers of extratidal stars in the Carina dwarf spheroidal galaxy. Such a large extratidal population, if conÐrmed, has implications not only for galaxy evolution but also for our understanding of the dark matter content of the dSph satellites. However, these surveys extend to much fainter magnitudes than previously possible, and it is important to understand possible contamination by foreground and background objects and the role of photometric errors at such faint levels.

Our essential result is that there are two major problems with the Washington luminosity classiÐcation : Ðrst, very metal-poor foreground subdwarfs are indistinguishable photometrically from halo giants ; second, photometric errors can scatter disk dwarfs into the halo giant region of the diagnostic plot. M[T 2 /M[51 In°2 we discuss possible contaminants of halo giant candidates in the diagram : disk and halo M[T 2 /M[51 dwarfs, galaxies, and quasi-stellar objects (QSOs). With accurate M[51 photometry, the only serious contaminants are the very metal-poor halo dwarfs whose weak lines make them indistinguishable photometrically from halo giants. We derive a luminosity function speciÐcally for such metalpoor halo dwarfs and use it with a simple halo model to predict the number of subdwarfs per square degree in di †erent directions in the Galaxy.

Although foreground disk and thick disk dwarfs are negligible contaminants if accurate photometry is obtained, the high density of these stars, especially at low latitudes, makes the number scattered into the giant region of the M[T 2 / M[51 diagram a sensitive function of photometric error. In°3 we investigate this in detail, and describe the double e †ect of large errors on giant searches : not only are dwarfs scattered into the giant region, but genuine giants are scattered out.

In°4 we use what we have learned about giant selection to examine our own pencil beam survey at high galactic latitudes (Paper II). The BTC subset (obtained using the Big Throughput Camera on the Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory [CTIO] 4 m telescope in 1999 April) covers 12.7 deg2 and has spectroscopic follow-up of approximately half of the giant candidates (Morrison et al. 2001). We Ðnd that foreground subdwarfs are the principal cause of our low detection efficiency for giants below V \ 18 and describe our plans to optimize future searches for the faint, red giants of the extreme outer halo so that fewer subdwarfs are misidentiÐed as giants.

In°5 we discuss the survey of MOPKJG of approximately 2 deg2 centered on the Carina dwarf spheroidal galaxy. Their study found a large number (D100) of giant candidates outside the tidal radius of Irwin & Hatzidimitriou (1995), but they were able only to obtain follow-up spectra of three of the brightest extratidal candidates. The photometric errors of the MPOKJG data are more typical of photographic than of CCD photometry, and we discuss the possible e †ect of these errors on the giant selection.  , which lies at the extreme blue end of our selection region. Binary Stars

Since up to 50% of all stars may be binaries, it is worth considering whether two stars in a binary system can masquerade as a single giant. This is trivially true of a binary system consisting of a giant and a faint dwarf companion, since the giantÏs luminosity will dominate. However, it is a little less clear whether a binary system composed of two main-sequence stars could have and M[51 colors M[T 2 within the giant region.

To test this we took the synthetic and M[51 M[T 2 colors of Paltoglou & Bell (1994) and of Bessell (2001) for stars with ranging from 4000 to 10000 K, log g from 4.5 T eff to 0.7, and [Fe/H] from 0 to [1.0, and combined them into simulated binary systems using the absolute magnitudes given in Bessell (2001). This is because (1) the bluer component of a binary made of two main-sequence stars will be brighter and so dominate the color and (2) it is not M[T 2 possible in a spectrum without emission lines to have M[51 signiÐcantly higher than 0.017 unless one star is extremely metal-poor.

Galaxies and QSOs

Because of the emission lines and redshifted features in galaxy and QSO spectra, these objects can be found both in  (1994) for very metal-poor stars reach no higher than M[51 \ 0.05, corresponding to the value that a blackbody spectrum would have. Thus, apart from photometric errors, we would not expect to see any normal or metal-poor stars with M[51 [ 0.05. The only other possibility is a spectrum that has less light, on average, in the wider M band than in the narrow DDO51 band close to its center. This can happen if absorption lines in a galaxyÏs spectrum are redshifted into the M band or if an emission line in a galaxy or QSO spectrum is redshifted into the DDO51 band. Figure 3 shows the spectrum of a BAL QSO identiÐed in our survey, with the M and DDO51 Ðlter passbands overlaid.5 The QSO spectrum is, to Ðrst order, featureless over the M passband, although part of the broad emission line at the blue end of the DDO51 passband would have been included in this ÐlterÏs observations, yielding the same or slightly more light per angstrom in the DDO51 Ðlter than in the wider M band.

In addition, the Washington colors of some normal galaxies are similar to those of metal-poor stars, so we will Ðnd a small number of galaxies in other regions of the M[T 2 versus M[51 diagram. Our survey uses data from mosaic CCD cameras (the Big Throughput Camera and the NOAO mosaics) on the KPNO and CTIO 4 m telescopes and the Burrell Schmidt telescope. We are particularly vulnerable to contamination by galaxies in our Schmidt data, where the large pixels make it more difficult to distinguish between stars and galaxies. There is still a small chance of contamination by compact galaxies and QSOs even in our better-sampled BTC and mosaic data. We discuss this further in°4. 3 for bluer stars. Although metal-poor giants lie further away from the dwarf locus because of their weak Mg b lines, this advantage is o †set by the fact that as we move to fainter magnitudes, foreground dwarfs become dominated by thick disk stars, whose lower metallicity ([Fe/H] D [0.5 ; Carney et al. 1989) moves them toward the giant region. Second, distant giants are strongly outnumbered by foreground disk stars, so we need to cope with the e †ect of 2 p and even 3 p errors on the dwarf colors.

We use the accurate Washington photometry obtained with the Big Throughput Camera (BTC) on the CTIO 4 m telescope in 1999 April (Paper II) to illustrate the e †ect of photometric errors on giant/dwarf classiÐcation. These pencil beam data cover 12.7 deg~2, with latitude ranging from b \ 25 to 72. For V \ 19, the median error in M[T 2 was 0.012 mag, and for M[51, 0.013 mag.

W here Do the Stars Go ?

To quantify the e †ect of photometric errors on our giant classiÐcations, we need to explore two e †ects : that of genuine giants removed from the giant region and that of dwarfs and other stars scattered into the giant region by color errors.

The Ðrst e †ect is simpler to quantify because it does not depend on the position in the Galaxy of the Ðeld surveyed. Figure 5 illustrates the movement of genuine giants in the diagram for the two classiÐcation schemes, M[51/M[T 2 assuming that each color was degraded by an amount drawn from a Gaussian with p \ 0.05 mag. Our smaller giant region leads to a higher loss rate of giants from the box. Figure 6 summarizes the percentage of giants lost ÈÈÈÈÈÈÈÈÈÈÈÈÈÈÈ 6 Often in astronomical data sets we do not have detailed information on the error distribution shape. In general, an error distribution with larger wings will produce more bogus giants, and a distribution with smaller wings than a Gaussian will have less e †ect. because of errors as a function of the color error. It can be seen that even for color errors as low as 0.02 mag around 20% of genuine giants will be lost. The most numerous (and least luminous) group of giant stars lie close to the blue boundary of our giant box at and the major-M[T 2 \ 1.1, ity of stars that are lost will be from this region. This e †ect and its dependence on color and absolute magnitude need be taken into account when using halo giants found with M[51 to measure the density distribution of the outer halo.

The leakage of foreground dwarfs into the giant regions is more complex to quantify, as it depends on the numbers of dwarfs close to the boundaries of the giant box. This is a strong function of galactic latitude in particular, since the path length of lower latitude lines of sight through the disk is longer. Figure 7 illustrates the regions of the color-color diagram where bogus giants originate for both classiÐcation schemes, in the case of 0.05 mag errors. (Only stars that will be observed in the giant selection regions will be followed.)  Figures 8 and 9 summarize the balance between the number of giants remaining in the giant region and the number of dwarfs moved into the giant region by photometric error, as a function of color error and galactic latitude. For these simulations we used the BTC data without error cuts, in the magnitude range V \ 16È19, which is typically the magnitude range we use to select giants in our survey (as spectroscopic follow-up becomes difficult fainter than V \ 19 on 4 mÈclass telescopes). The absence of error cuts is because we need to measure how many dwarf stars are in the correct color and magnitude ranges to be moved into the giant region via photometric errors, and limiting the data selected via our errors will lead to incompleteness \ 1.0. This latter requirement will cause some blue giants to be included, but the M[51 color holds no information about luminosity this blue. To give a feeling for how important this is with respect to the actual numbers of halo giants likely to be found (in a smooth halo) we have used the predictions of the halo model of Morrison (1993) for each latitude bin and the same magnitude range. (These predictions agree in general with the numbers of halo giants that we have found in our survey Ðelds.) The number of halo giants falls as the error increases because more giants get scattered out of the halo region.

It can be seen from the plots that, especially for low latitudes, large numbers of dwarfs are scattered into the giant box. For our classiÐcation scheme, the 50% success point, where the number of dwarfs scattered in equals the number of giants not scattered out of the giant box, occurs for color errors between 0.035 and 0.045 mag. For the larger giant box of MOKP, the e †ect is extremeÈbogus giants outnumber genuine ones for color errors greater than 0.02 mag. The number of giant candidates that are actually dwarfs can reach more than 100 deg~2 for large errors and lower latitudes. It is clear that spectroscopic follow-up of every giant candidate to conÐrm its luminosity is vitally important. Without it, spurious conclusions will surely result. With this background behind us, we now consider implications for our own survey and that of MOPKJG.
EXAMPLE 1 : SPECTROSCOPIC FOLLOW-UP OF OUR BTC DATA

Here we describe our spectroscopic follow-up of the BTC imaging data of 12.7 deg2 (Paper II), focusing on the dwarfs and other contaminants that we identiÐed. (In a future paper, Morrison et al. 2001, we will describe our spectroscopic calibrations to measure luminosity and metallicity in detail.) In three observing runs on the KPNO 4 m telescope (in 1999 May, 2000 January, and 2000 March) we observed and classiÐed 57 halo giant candidates, with V magnitudes ranging from to 19.2. This constitutes approx-V 0 \ 15.6 imately 50% of our giant candidates in the BTC data.
One candidate (with was a QSO ; so far we V 0 \ 18.7) have found no galaxies in our BTC data because of the good spatial sampling of the BTC CCDs.
Foreground Dwarfs

We have estimated the metallicity of the foreground dwarfs that we identiÐed, by comparing their Mg b/MgH line strength at the observed color with that of the M[T 2 dwarf and subdwarf standards observed on these runs (see Table 1 above and Table 2 of Morrison et al. 2000). This allowed us to classify them as subdwarfs with [Fe/H] \ [2.0 or as metal-richer dwarfs and subdwarfs.
Extreme Subdwarfs

Out of the 57 halo giant candidates observed, 22 were subdwarfs. (Our giant selection criteria have evolved as we learned more about metal-poor subdwarfs, so some of these stars have colors that place them outside our giant selection box.) Figure 10 shows the histogram of V magnitudes of the 57 halo candidates observed, with the histogram of subdwarf magnitudes overlaid. The magnitude distribution of halo candidates observed reÑects the weather and seeing during our 4 m spectroscopic runs rather than the true distribution of halo giants. The sample size is small, but it is still possible to see that the proportion of subdwarfs increases as we go to fainter magnitudes. In summary, our spectroscopic follow-up has conÐrmed the importance of accurate photometry for giant selection using the Washington system. In addition, the number of subdwarfs found in our Ðelds is in agreement with the predictions of the model described in°2.2 and the Appendix. Particularly for V magnitudes fainter than 18, photometric identiÐcation of halo giants is not enough : spectroscopic conÐrmation of their luminosity is very important.
Efficiently Selecting Faint Giants

If we observe spectroscopically every giant candidate that appears in the giant region of Figure 15 (see Appendix) for V fainter than 18, we will Ðnd three subdwarfs for every genuine halo giant. The stars that are of particular interest in this magnitude range are the high-luminosity giants that help trace the extreme outer halo, such as our star l304.49b]60.51 (Olszewski et al. 2001). With accurate photometry, it is possible to make our spectroscopic follow-up more efficient by utilizing the sensitivity of the M[51 color to luminosity. Figure 12 shows the halo giants and subdwarfs identiÐed by spectroscopic follow-up, with giants coded by absolute magnitude. E †ect of Photometric Errors

Carina has quite a low galactic latitude (b \ 22) so there are large numbers of disk stars in the foreground, and the potential exists for a signiÐcant number to scatter into the giant region of the diagram. The accuracy of M[T 2 /M[51 the MOPKJG photometry is not high. This is caused in great part by their short exposure times : their C40 telescope exposure times in M and were almost the same as our T 2 4 m BTC exposure times, 15 times shorter when the di †erence in aperture is taken into account. (Their DDO51 exposures were a factor of D3 shorter after correcting for telescope aperture.) MOPKJG work more than a magnitude fainter than our survey, to M \ 20.8 (V^20.5). In addition, the C100 data su †ered from such large pointspread function (PSF) variations that even a quadratic variable PSF in DAOPHOT was unable to correct them completely.

To deal with these large errors they restrict consideration to stars with error estimates in all Ðlters less than 0.10 mag. Thus it is possible for stars with color errors as high as 0.14 mag in M[51 or to be included in their sample. In M[T 2 Figure 9 we showed that at latitudes of 30¡È40¡, signiÐcantly higher than the latitude of Carina, almost 200 dwarf stars per square degree are scattered into the MOKP giant box for color errors of 0.10 mag. Thus the additional cut using the Carina giant branch is very important.

MOPKJG estimate the contribution of "" background ÏÏ objects by successively displacing the Carina giant branch region to brighter magnitudes and counting how many stars that satisfy their cut are found in the shifted M[51/M[T 2 giant branch region. Their decision to shift the box only to brighter magnitudes is forced upon them by the serious incompleteness of their photometry at magnitudes fainter than M \ 20.8. This is unfortunate, because the number of interlopers in the giant region increases sharply at fainter magnitudes, so their background estimates will be systematically too small.

The magnitude range of interest for Carina giants is Here, the majority of the C100 photometry stars having errors in each Ðlter close to this number, color errors of up to 0.14 mag are likely. We have extended our simulations of the likely number of foreground dwarfs that will be moved into the MOKP giant selection box in the diagram by adding the same selection as M[51/M[T 2 that used by MOPKJG (the CMD bounding box outlined in their Figure 8) to isolate stars at the right color and magnitude to be on CarinaÏs giant branch. Figure 13 shows our results. It can be seen that with color errors in the range of 0.05 to 0.10 mag, dwarf contamination is signiÐcantly higher than that claimed by MOPKJG, whose largest extratidal background estimate was 22 stars per square degree.

In summary, more spectroscopic follow-up is needed to conÐrm the claim of MOPKJG that Carina is losing 27% of its mass per gigayear. With photometric errors of 0.10 mag, the typical star in the giant region will be a photometric error. Brighter stars, such as the three observed spectroscopically, will have smaller photometric errors and will in general be giants if they are in the giant region. However, only one of these is more than 2 p away from the Irwin & Hatzidimitriou (1995) tidal radius. A larger spectroscopic sample is needed. The discovery of one extratidal bright giant tells us nothing about the discovery fraction of fainter giants.
SUMMARY

Washington photometry, with the addition of the DDO51 Ðlter, is a powerful method of Ðnding distant halo giants. We Ðnd that at the faintest magnitudes probed by our survey, our giant selection efficiency falls, and we make a careful examination of possible problems with the Washington giant classiÐcation to improve future surveys. We show that accurate photometry (color errors less than 0.03 mag) is essential to cut down on the scattering of the numerous foreground dwarfs into the giant region in the color-color plot. We have made estimates of M[51/M[T 2 the contamination of giant candidates by very metal-poor halo dwarfs by deriving a new luminosity function speciÐcally for the subdwarfs that mimic halo giants in the diagram and by using it in a simple halo M[51/M[T 2 model.

We used our results on luminosity discrimination with the Washington system to examine two recent surveys : our own survey of 12.7 deg2 at high galactic latitudes Paper II) and the study of MOPKJG of Ðelds centered on the Carina dwarf spheroidal galaxy, which Ðnds over 100 Carina-associated giant candidates outside its tidal radius.

For surveys such as our own of the halo Ðeld, very metalpoor halo dwarfs are the major source of contamination of candidate giant samples, and we propose using a smaller region of the diagram to optimize spectro-M[51/M[T 2 scopic follow-up at the faint magnitudes where the subdwarfs dominate. The survey of MOPKJG has spectroscopic follow-up for only three of the brightest "" extratidal ÏÏ giant candidates, and we show that their photometric errors, which increase as stars become fainter, can have a very serious e †ect on their giant classiÐcation.

In summary, spectroscopic follow-up of giant stars identi-Ðed using the Washington system is vital. If one wishes to make statistical corrections for the number of bogus giants caused by photometric errors, it is important to quantify accurately the photometric errors in the data, both in terms of the size of the average error and the shape of the distribution.
